[335](https://docs.rs#335)
[336](https://docs.rs#336)/// The outcome of performing a test/benchmark.
[337](https://docs.rs#337)#[derive(Debug, Clone)]
[338](https://docs.rs#338)enum Outcome {
[339](https://docs.rs#339)    /// The test passed.
[340](https://docs.rs#340)    Passed,
[341](https://docs.rs#341)
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    /// The test or benchmark failed.
[343](https://docs.rs#343)    Failed(Failed),
[344](https://docs.rs#344)
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    /// The test or benchmark was ignored.
[346](https://docs.rs#346)    Ignored,
[347](https://docs.rs#347)
[348](https://docs.rs#348)    /// The test or benchmark was ignored.
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    RuntimeIgnored { reason: Option<String> },
[350](https://docs.rs#350)
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    /// The benchmark was successfully run.
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    Measured(Measurement),
[353](https://docs.rs#353)}
[354](https://docs.rs#354)
[355](https://docs.rs#355)/// Contains information about the entire test run. Is returned by[`run`].
[356](https://docs.rs#356)///
[357](https://docs.rs#357)/// This type is marked as `#[must_use]`. Usually, you just call
[358](https://docs.rs#358)/// [`exit()`][Conclusion::exit] on the result of `run` to exit the application
[359](https://docs.rs#359)/// with the correct exit code. But you can also store this value and inspect
[360](https://docs.rs#360)/// its data.
[361](https://docs.rs#361)#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
[362](https://docs.rs#362)#[must_use = "Call `exit()` or `exit_if_failed()` to set the correct return code"]
[363](https://docs.rs#363)pub struct Conclusion {
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    /// Number of tests and benchmarks that were filtered out (either by the
[365](https://docs.rs#365)    /// filter-in pattern or by `--skip` arguments).
[366](https://docs.rs#366)    pub num_filtered_out: u64,
[367](https://docs.rs#367)
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    /// Number of passed tests.
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    pub num_passed: u64,
[370](https://docs.rs#370)
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    /// Number of failed tests and benchmarks.
[372](https://docs.rs#372)    pub num_failed: u64,
[373](https://docs.rs#373)
[374](https://docs.rs#374)    /// Number of ignored tests and benchmarks.
[375](https://docs.rs#375)    pub num_ignored: u64,
[376](https://docs.rs#376)
[377](https://docs.rs#377)    /// Number of benchmarks that successfully ran.
[378](https://docs.rs#378)    pub num_measured: u64,
[379](https://docs.rs#379)}
[380](https://docs.rs#380)
[381](https://docs.rs#381)impl Conclusion {
[382](https://docs.rs#382)    /// Returns an exit code that can be returned from `main` to signal
[383](https://docs.rs#383)    /// success/failure to the calling process.
[384](https://docs.rs#384)    pub fn exit_code(&self) -> ExitCode {
[385](https://docs.rs#385)        if self.has_failed() {
[386](https://docs.rs#386)            ExitCode::from(101)
[387](https://docs.rs#387)        } else {
[388](https://docs.rs#388)            ExitCode::SUCCESS
[389](https://docs.rs#389)        }
[390](https://docs.rs#390)    }
[391](https://docs.rs#391)
[392](https://docs.rs#392)    /// Returns whether there have been any failures.
[393](https://docs.rs#393)    pub fn has_failed(&self) -> bool {
[394](https://docs.rs#394)        self.num_failed > 0
[395](https://docs.rs#395)    }
[396](https://docs.rs#396)
[397](https://docs.rs#397)    /// Exits the application with an appropriate error code (0 if all tests
[398](https://docs.rs#398)    /// have passed, 101 if there have been failures). This uses
[399](https://docs.rs#399)    /// [`process::exit`], meaning that destructors are not ran. Consider
[400](https://docs.rs#400)    /// using [`Self::exit_code`] instead for a proper program cleanup.
[401](https://docs.rs#401)    pub fn exit(&self) -> ! {
[402](https://docs.rs#402)        self.exit_if_failed();
[403](https://docs.rs#403)        process::exit(0);
[404](https://docs.rs#404)    }
[405](https://docs.rs#405)
[406](https://docs.rs#406)    /// Exits the application with error code 101 if there were any failures.
[407](https://docs.rs#407)    /// Otherwise, returns normally. This uses [`process::exit`], meaning that
[408](https://docs.rs#408)    /// destructors are not ran. Consider using [`Self::exit_code`] instead for
[409](https://docs.rs#409)    /// a proper program cleanup.
[410](https://docs.rs#410)    pub fn exit_if_failed(&self) {
[411](https://docs.rs#411)        if self.has_failed() {
[412](https://docs.rs#412)            process::exit(101)
[413](https://docs.rs#413)        }
[414](https://docs.rs#414)    }
[415](https://docs.rs#415)
[416](https://docs.rs#416)    fn empty() -> Self {
[417](https://docs.rs#417)        Self {
[418](https://docs.rs#418)            num_filtered_out: 0,
[419](https://docs.rs#419)            num_passed: 0,
[420](https://docs.rs#420)            num_failed: 0,
[421](https://docs.rs#421)            num_ignored: 0,
[422](https://docs.rs#422)            num_measured: 0,
[423](https://docs.rs#423)        }
[424](https://docs.rs#424)    }
[425](https://docs.rs#425)}
[426](https://docs.rs#426)
[427](https://docs.rs#427)impl Arguments {
[428](https://docs.rs#428)    /// Returns `true` if the given trial should be ignored by these arguments.
[429](https://docs.rs#429)    ///
[430](https://docs.rs#430)    /// Ignored tests are not run, but still listed in the outcome.
[431](https://docs.rs#431)    pub fn is_ignored(&self, test: &Trial) -> bool {
[432](https://docs.rs#432)        (test.info.is_ignored && !self.ignored && !self.include_ignored)
[433](https://docs.rs#433)            || (test.info.is_bench && self.test)
[434](https://docs.rs#434)            || (!test.info.is_bench && self.bench)
[435](https://docs.rs#435)    }
[436](https://docs.rs#436)
[437](https://docs.rs#437)    /// Returns `true` if the given trial should be filtered out by these
[438](https://docs.rs#438)    /// arguments.
[439](https://docs.rs#439)    pub fn is_filtered_out(&self, test: &Trial) -> bool {
[440](https://docs.rs#440)        let test_name = test.name();
[441](https://docs.rs#441)        // Match against the full test name, including the kind. This upholds the invariant that if
[442](https://docs.rs#442)        // --list prints out:
[443](https://docs.rs#443)        //
[444](https://docs.rs#444)        // <some string>: test
[445](https://docs.rs#445)        //
[446](https://docs.rs#446)        // then "--exact <some string>" runs exactly that test.
[447](https://docs.rs#447)        let test_name_with_kind = test.info.test_name_with_kind();
[448](https://docs.rs#448)
[449](https://docs.rs#449)        // If a filter was specified, apply this
[450](https://docs.rs#450)        if let Some(filter) = &self.filter {
[451](https://docs.rs#451)            match self.exact {
[452](https://docs.rs#452)                // For exact matches, we want to match against either the test name (to maintain
[453](https://docs.rs#453)                // backwards compatibility with older versions of libtest-mimic), or the test kind
[454](https://docs.rs#454)                // (technically more correct with respect to matching against the output of --list.)
[455](https://docs.rs#455)                true if test_name != filter && &test_name_with_kind != filter => return true,
[456](https://docs.rs#456)                false if !test_name_with_kind.contains(filter) => return true,
[457](https://docs.rs#457)                _ => {}
[458](https://docs.rs#458)            };
[459](https://docs.rs#459)        }
[460](https://docs.rs#460)
[461](https://docs.rs#461)        // If any skip pattern were specified, test for all patterns.
[462](https://docs.rs#462)        for skip_filter in &self.skip {
[463](https://docs.rs#463)            match self.exact {
[464](https://docs.rs#464)                // For exact matches, we want to match against either the test name (to maintain
[465](https://docs.rs#465)                // backwards compatibility with older versions of libtest-mimic), or the test kind
[466](https://docs.rs#466)                // (technically more correct with respect to matching against the output of --list.)
[467](https://docs.rs#467)                true if test_name == skip_filter || &test_name_with_kind == skip_filter => {
[468](https://docs.rs#468)                    return true
[469](https://docs.rs#469)                }
[470](https://docs.rs#470)                false if test_name_with_kind.contains(skip_filter) => return true,
[471](https://docs.rs#471)                _ => {}
[472](https://docs.rs#472)            }
[473](https://docs.rs#473)        }
[474](https://docs.rs#474)
[475](https://docs.rs#475)        if self.ignored && !test.info.is_ignored {
[476](https://docs.rs#476)            return true;
[477](https://docs.rs#477)        }
[478](https://docs.rs#478)
[479](https://docs.rs#479)        false
[480](https://docs.rs#480)    }

[483](https://docs.rs#483)/// Runs all given trials (tests & benchmarks).
[484](https://docs.rs#484)///
[485](https://docs.rs#485)/// This is the central function of this crate. It provides the framework for
[486](https://docs.rs#486)/// the testing harness. It does all the printing and house keeping.
[487](https://docs.rs#487)///
[488](https://docs.rs#488)/// The returned value contains a couple of useful information. See
[489](https://docs.rs#489)/// [`Conclusion`] for more information. If `--list` was specified, a list is
[490](https://docs.rs#490)/// printed and a dummy `Conclusion` is returned.
[491](https://docs.rs#491)pub fn run(args: &Arguments, mut tests: Vec<Trial>) -> Conclusion {
[492](https://docs.rs#492)    let start_instant = Instant::now();
[493](https://docs.rs#493)    let mut conclusion = Conclusion::empty();
[494](https://docs.rs#494)
[495](https://docs.rs#495)    // Apply filtering
[496](https://docs.rs#496)    if args.filter.is_some() || !args.skip.is_empty() || args.ignored {
[497](https://docs.rs#497)        let len_before = tests.len() as u64;
[498](https://docs.rs#498)        tests.retain(|test| !args.is_filtered_out(test));
[499](https://docs.rs#499)        conclusion.num_filtered_out = len_before - tests.len() as u64;
[500](https://docs.rs#500)    }
[501](https://docs.rs#501)    let tests = tests;
[502](https://docs.rs#502)
[503](https://docs.rs#503)    // Create printer which is used for all output.
[504](https://docs.rs#504)    let mut printer = printer::Printer::new(args, &tests);
[505](https://docs.rs#505)
[506](https://docs.rs#506)    // If `--list` is specified, just print the list and return.
[507](https://docs.rs#507)    if args.list {
[508](https://docs.rs#508)        printer.print_list(&tests, args.ignored);
[509](https://docs.rs#509)        return Conclusion::empty();
[510](https://docs.rs#510)    }
[511](https://docs.rs#511)
[512](https://docs.rs#512)    // Print number of tests
[513](https://docs.rs#513)    printer.print_title(tests.len() as u64);
[514](https://docs.rs#514)
[515](https://docs.rs#515)    let mut failed_tests = Vec::new();
[516](https://docs.rs#516)    let mut handle_outcome = |outcome: Outcome, test: TestInfo, printer: &mut Printer| {
[517](https://docs.rs#517)        printer.print_single_outcome(&test, &outcome);
[518](https://docs.rs#518)
[519](https://docs.rs#519)        // Handle outcome
[520](https://docs.rs#520)        match outcome {
[521](https://docs.rs#521)            Outcome::Passed => conclusion.num_passed += 1,
[522](https://docs.rs#522)            Outcome::Failed(failed) => {
[523](https://docs.rs#523)                failed_tests.push((test, failed.msg));
[524](https://docs.rs#524)                conclusion.num_failed += 1;
[525](https://docs.rs#525)            }
[526](https://docs.rs#526)            Outcome::Ignored => conclusion.num_ignored += 1,
[527](https://docs.rs#527)            Outcome::Measured(_) => conclusion.num_measured += 1,
[528](https://docs.rs#528)            Outcome::RuntimeIgnored { .. } => conclusion.num_ignored += 1,
[529](https://docs.rs#529)        }
[530](https://docs.rs#530)    };
[531](https://docs.rs#531)
[532](https://docs.rs#532)    // Execute all tests.
[533](https://docs.rs#533)    let test_mode = !args.bench;
[534](https://docs.rs#534)
[535](https://docs.rs#535)    let num_threads = platform_defaults_to_one_thread()
[536](https://docs.rs#536)        .then_some(1)
[537](https://docs.rs#537)        .or(args.test_threads)
[538](https://docs.rs#538)        .or_else(|| std::thread::available_parallelism().ok().map(Into::into))
[539](https://docs.rs#539)        .unwrap_or(1);
[540](https://docs.rs#540)
[541](https://docs.rs#541)    if num_threads == 1 {
[542](https://docs.rs#542)        // Run test sequentially in main thread
[543](https://docs.rs#543)        for test in tests {
[544](https://docs.rs#544)            // Print `test foo    ...`, run the test, then print the outcome in
[545](https://docs.rs#545)            // the same line.
[546](https://docs.rs#546)            printer.print_test(&test.info);
[547](https://docs.rs#547)            let outcome = if args.is_ignored(&test) {
[548](https://docs.rs#548)                Outcome::Ignored
[549](https://docs.rs#549)            } else {
[550](https://docs.rs#550)                run_single(test.runner, test_mode)
[551](https://docs.rs#551)            };
[552](https://docs.rs#552)            handle_outcome(outcome, test.info, &mut printer);
[553](https://docs.rs#553)        }
[554](https://docs.rs#554)    } else {
[555](https://docs.rs#555)        // Run test in thread pool.
[556](https://docs.rs#556)        let (sender, receiver) = mpsc::channel();
[557](https://docs.rs#557)
[558](https://docs.rs#558)        let num_tests = tests.len();
[559](https://docs.rs#559)        // TODO: this should use a mpmc channel, once that's stabilized in std.
[560](https://docs.rs#560)        let iter = Mutex::new(tests.into_iter());
[561](https://docs.rs#561)        thread::scope(|scope| {
[562](https://docs.rs#562)            // Start worker threads
[563](https://docs.rs#563)            for _ in 0..num_threads {
[564](https://docs.rs#564)                scope.spawn(|| {
[565](https://docs.rs#565)                    loop {
[566](https://docs.rs#566)                        // Get next test to process from the iterator.
[567](https://docs.rs#567)                        let Some(trial) = iter.lock().unwrap().next() else {
[568](https://docs.rs#568)                            break;
[569](https://docs.rs#569)                        };
[570](https://docs.rs#570)
[571](https://docs.rs#571)                        let payload = if args.is_ignored(&trial) {
[572](https://docs.rs#572)                            (Outcome::Ignored, trial.info)
[573](https://docs.rs#573)                        } else {
[574](https://docs.rs#574)                            let outcome = run_single(trial.runner, test_mode);
[575](https://docs.rs#575)                            (outcome, trial.info)
[576](https://docs.rs#576)                        };
[577](https://docs.rs#577)
[578](https://docs.rs#578)                        // It's fine to ignore the result of sending. If the
[579](https://docs.rs#579)                        // receiver has hung up, everything will wind down soon
[580](https://docs.rs#580)                        // anyway.
[581](https://docs.rs#581)                        let _ = sender.send(payload);
[582](https://docs.rs#582)                    }
[583](https://docs.rs#583)                });
[584](https://docs.rs#584)            }
[585](https://docs.rs#585)
[586](https://docs.rs#586)            // Print results of tests that already dinished
[587](https://docs.rs#587)            for (outcome, test_info) in receiver.iter().take(num_tests) {
[588](https://docs.rs#588)                // In multithreaded mode, we do only print the start of the line
[589](https://docs.rs#589)                // after the test ran, as otherwise it would lead to terribly
[590](https://docs.rs#590)                // interleaved output.
[591](https://docs.rs#591)                printer.print_test(&test_info);
[592](https://docs.rs#592)                handle_outcome(outcome, test_info, &mut printer);
[593](https://docs.rs#593)            }
[594](https://docs.rs#594)        });
[595](https://docs.rs#595)
[596](https://docs.rs#596)    }
[597](https://docs.rs#597)
[598](https://docs.rs#598)    // Print failures if there were any, and the final summary.
[599](https://docs.rs#599)    if !failed_tests.is_empty() {
[600](https://docs.rs#600)        printer.print_failures(&failed_tests);
[601](https://docs.rs#601)    }
[602](https://docs.rs#602)
[603](https://docs.rs#603)    printer.print_summary(&conclusion, start_instant.elapsed());
[604](https://docs.rs#604)
[605](https://docs.rs#605)    conclusion
[606](https://docs.rs#606)}
[607](https://docs.rs#607)
[608](https://docs.rs#608)/// Returns whether the current host platform should use a single thread by
[609](https://docs.rs#609)/// default rather than a thread pool by default. Some platforms, such as
[610](https://docs.rs#610)/// WebAssembly, don't have native support for threading at this time.
[611](https://docs.rs#611)fn platform_defaults_to_one_thread() -> bool {
[612](https://docs.rs#612)    cfg!(target_family = "wasm")
[613](https://docs.rs#613)}
[614](https://docs.rs#614)
[615](https://docs.rs#615)/// Runs the given runner, catching any panics and treating them as a failed test.
[616](https://docs.rs#616)fn run_single(runner: Box<dyn FnOnce(bool) -> Outcome + Send>, test_mode: bool) -> Outcome {
[617](https://docs.rs#617)    use std::panic::{catch_unwind, AssertUnwindSafe};
[618](https://docs.rs#618)
[619](https://docs.rs#619)    catch_unwind(AssertUnwindSafe(move || runner(test_mode))).unwrap_or_else(|e| {
[620](https://docs.rs#620)        // The `panic` information is just an `Any` object representing the
[621](https://docs.rs#621)        // value the panic was invoked with. For most panics (which use
[622](https://docs.rs#622)        // `panic!` like `println!`), this is either `&str` or `String`.
[623](https://docs.rs#623)        let payload = e.downcast_ref::<String>()
[624](https://docs.rs#624)            .map(|s| s.as_str())
[625](https://docs.rs#625)            .or(e.downcast_ref::<&str>().map(|s| *s));
[626](https://docs.rs#626)
[627](https://docs.rs#627)        let msg = match payload {
[628](https://docs.rs#628)            Some(payload) => format!("test panicked: {payload}"),
[629](https://docs.rs#629)            None => format!("test panicked"),
[630](https://docs.rs#630)        };
[631](https://docs.rs#631)        Outcome::Failed(msg.into())
[632](https://docs.rs#632)    })
[633](https://docs.rs#633)}

# Trial in libtest_mimic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libtest-mimic/0.8.2/libtest_mimic/struct.Trial.html

`pub struct Trial { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

A single test or benchmark.

The original `libtest` often calls benchmarks “tests”, which is a bit
confusing. So in this library, it is called “trial”.

A trial is created via [ Trial::test](https://docs.rs/struct.Trial.html#method.test) or

[. The trial’s](https://docs.rs/struct.Trial.html#method.bench)

`Trial::bench``name` is printed and used for filtering. The `runner` is called when the
test/benchmark is executed to determine its outcome. If `runner` panics,
the trial is considered “failed”. If you need the behavior of
`#[should_panic]` you need to catch the panic yourself. You likely want to
compare the panic payload to an expected value anyway.## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

Creates a (non-benchmark) test with the given name and runner.

The runner returning `Ok(())` is interpreted as the test passing. If the
runner returns `Err(_)`, the test is considered failed.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/libtest_mimic/lib.rs.html#148-165)#### pub fn [ignorable_test](https://docs.rs#method.ignorable_test)<R>(name: impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>, runner: R) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/libtest_mimic/lib.rs.html#148-165)

#### pub fn [ignorable_test](https://docs.rs#method.ignorable_test)<R>(name: impl [Into](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.Into.html)<[String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)>, runner: R) -> Self

Creates a test like [ Self::test](https://docs.rs/struct.Trial.html#method.test), but with a runner that can decide to
ignore the test.

Like other tests, returning an `Err` is a test failure. The `Ok` variant for this test must
return a [ Completion](https://docs.rs/enum.Completion.html) to indicate whether the test successfully ran to completion, or if
it was ignored at some point during testing. If it was skipped, a reason may be provided.

Creates a benchmark with the given name and runner.

If the runner’s parameter `test_mode` is `true`, the runner function
should run all code just once, without measuring, just to make sure it
does not panic. If the parameter is `false`, it should perform the
actual benchmark. If `test_mode` is `true` you may return `Ok(None)`,
but if it’s `false`, you have to return a `Measurement`, or else the
benchmark is considered a failure.

`test_mode` is `true` if neither `--bench` nor `--test` are set, and
`false` when `--bench` is set. If `--test` is set, benchmarks are not
ran at all, and both flags cannot be set at the same time.

Sets the “kind” of this test/benchmark. If this string is not
empty, it is printed in brackets before the test name (e.g.
`test [my-kind] test_name`). (Default: *empty*)

This is the only extension to the original libtest.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/libtest_mimic/lib.rs.html#221-229)#### pub fn [with_ignored_flag](https://docs.rs#method.with_ignored_flag)(self, is_ignored: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/libtest_mimic/lib.rs.html#221-229)

#### pub fn [with_ignored_flag](https://docs.rs#method.with_ignored_flag)(self, is_ignored: [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)) -> Self

Sets whether or not this test is considered “ignored”. (Default: `false`)

With the built-in test suite, you can annotate `#[ignore]` on tests to
not execute them by default (for example because they take a long time
or require a special environment). If the `--ignored` flag is set,
ignored tests are executed, too.

Returns the kind of this trial. If you have not set a kind, this is an empty string.

Command line arguments.

This type represents everything the user can specify via CLI args. The main
method is [ from_args](https://docs.rs/struct.Arguments.html#method.from_args) which reads the global

`std::env::args()` and parses them into this type.`libtest-mimic` supports a subset of all args/flags supported by the
official test harness. There are also some other minor CLI differences, but
the main use cases should work exactly like with the built-in harness.

### impl [Conclusion](https://docs.rs/struct.Conclusion.html)

Returns an exit code that can be returned from `main` to signal
success/failure to the calling process.

Exits the application with an appropriate error code (0 if all tests
have passed, 101 if there have been failures). This uses
[ process::exit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/fn.exit.html), meaning that destructors are not ran. Consider
using

[instead for a proper program cleanup.](https://docs.rs/struct.Conclusion.html#method.exit_code)

#### pub fn [exit_if_failed](https://docs.rs#method.exit_if_failed)(&self)

Otherwise, returns normally. This uses [ process::exit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/process/fn.exit.html), meaning that
destructors are not ran. Consider using

# libtest_mimic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libtest-mimic/latest/libtest_mimic/

## Expand description

Write your own tests and benchmarks that look and behave like built-in tests!

This is a simple and small test harness that mimics the original `libtest`
(used by `cargo test`/`rustc --test`). That means: all output looks pretty
much like `cargo test` and most CLI arguments are understood and used. With
that plumbing work out of the way, your test runner can focus on the actual
testing.

For a small real world example, see [ examples/tidy.rs](https://github.com/LukasKalbertodt/libtest-mimic/blob/master/examples/tidy.rs).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

To use this, you most likely want to add a manual `[[test]]` section to
`Cargo.toml` and set `harness = false`. For example:

```
[[test]]
name = "mytest"
path = "tests/mytest.rs"
harness = false
```
And in `tests/mytest.rs` you would call [ run](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html) in the

`main` function:```
use libtest_mimic::{Arguments, Trial};
// Parse command line arguments
let args = Arguments::from_args();
// Create a list of tests and/or benchmarks (in this case: two dummy tests).
let tests = vec![
    Trial::test("succeeding_test", move || Ok(())),
    Trial::test("failing_test", move || Err("Woops".into())),
];
// Run all tests and exit the application appropriatly.
libtest_mimic::run(&args, tests).exit();
```
Instead of returning `Ok` or `Err` directly, you want to actually perform
your tests, of course. See [ Trial::test](https://docs.rs/struct.Trial.html#method.test) for more information on how to
define a test. You can of course list all your tests manually. But in many
cases it is useful to generate one test per file in a directory, for
example.

You can then run `cargo test --test mytest` to run it. To see the CLI
arguments supported by this crate, run `cargo test --test mytest -- -h`.

[§](https://docs.rs#known-limitations-and-differences-to-the-official-test-harness)Known limitations and differences to the official test harness

`libtest-mimic` works on a best-effort basis: it tries to be as close to
`libtest` as possible, but there are differences for a variety of reasons.
For example, some rarely used features might not be implemented, some
features are extremely difficult to implement, and removing minor,
unimportant differences is just not worth the hassle.

Some of the notable differences:

- Output capture and `--nocapture`: simply not supported. The official`libtest`uses internal`std`functions to temporarily redirect output.`libtest-mimic`cannot use those. See[this issue](https://github.com/LukasKalbertodt/libtest-mimic/issues/9)for more information.
- `--format=junit`
- Also see [#13](https://github.com/LukasKalbertodt/libtest-mimic/issues/13)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arguments](https://docs.rs/struct.Arguments.html)
- Command line arguments.
- [Conclusion](https://docs.rs/struct.Conclusion.html)
- Contains information about the entire test run. Is returned by`run`
- [Failed](https://docs.rs/struct.Failed.html)
- Indicates that a test/benchmark has failed. Optionally carries a message.
- [Measurement](https://docs.rs/struct.Measurement.html)
- Output of a benchmark.
- [Trial](https://docs.rs/struct.Trial.html)
- A single test or benchmark.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorSetting.html)- Setting
- Possible values for the `--color`option.
- [Completion](https://docs.rs/enum.Completion.html)
- A representation of whether a test ran to completion or was ignored during its runtime.
- [Format](https://docs.rs/enum.FormatSetting.html)- Setting
- Possible values for the `--format`option.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [run](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html)
- Runs all given trials (tests & benchmarks).

# libtest-mimic 0.8.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/libtest-mimic/latest/builds

All the builds on docs.rs are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The limits for this crate are the following:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                    If a build fails because it hit one of those limits please
                    [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                    to get them increased.

# anstream 1.0.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/anstream/^1

# anstream

A simple cross platform library for writing colored text to a terminal.

*A portmanteau of "ansi stream"*

Specialized `stdout` and `stderr` that accept ANSI escape codes and adapt them
based on the terminal's capabilities.

`anstream::adapter::strip_str` may also be of interest on its own for low
overhead stripping of ANSI escape codes.

# anstyle

ANSI text styling

*A portmanteau of "ansi style"*

`anstyle` provides core types describing [ANSI styling escape
codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code) for interoperability
between crates.  For example, this would allow a crate to provide an API for
customizing the colors used without putting the underlying text styling crate
in the API.

For integration with your text styling crate, see:

General utilities:

- [anstyle-git](https://docs.rs/crates/git): Parse Git style descriptions

# escape8259 0.5.3 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/escape8259/^0.5.2

`escape8259` performs RFC8259-compliant string escaping and un-escaping.

[RFC8259](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc8259) is a JSON encoding standard.  Many JSON encoders exist, but other
RFCs use the same string escaping mechanism, so it's useful to be able to
access the string escaping functions by themselves.

# Examples

```
use ;
let s = "A null (\0) and a double-quote (\")";
assert_eq!;
let crab = r#"This is a crab: \ud83e\udd80"#;
assert_eq!;
// We accept encodings that weren't really necessary.
assert_eq!;
let multiline = r#"hello
 world"#;
assert_eq!;
```

# fastrand 2.4.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/fastrand/^2.0.0

# fastrand

A simple and fast random number generator.

The implementation uses [Wyrand](https://github.com/wangyi-fudan/wyhash), a simple and fast
generator but **not** cryptographically secure.

## Examples

Flip a coin:

```
if bool  else
```
Generate a random `i32`:

```
let num = i32;
```
Choose a random element in an array:

```
let v = vec!;
let i = usize;
let elem = v;
```
Sample values from an array with `O(n)` complexity (`n` is the length of array):

```
choose_multiple;
choose_multiple;
```
Shuffle an array:

```
let mut v = vec!;
shuffle;
```
Generate a random `Vec` or `String`:

```
use repeat_with;
let v:  = repeat_with.take.collect;
let s: String = repeat_with.take.collect;
```
To get reproducible results on every run, initialize the generator with a seed:

```
// Pick an arbitrary number as seed.
seed;
// Now this prints the same number on every run:
println!;
```
To be more efficient, create a new `Rng` instance instead of using the thread-local
generator:

```
use repeat_with;
let rng = new;
let mut bytes:  = repeat_with.take.collect;
```
This crate aims to expose a core set of useful randomness primitives. For more niche algorithms, consider using the [ fastrand-contrib](https://crates.io/crates/fastrand-contrib) crate alongside this one.

# Features

- `std`(enabled by default): Enables the- `std`library. This is required for the global generator and global entropy. Without this feature, [- `Rng`] can only be instantiated using the- `with_seed`
- `js`: Assumes that WebAssembly targets are being run in a JavaScript environment.

# pretty_assertions 1.4.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/pretty_assertions/^1.2.1

# Pretty Assertions

Overwrite `assert_eq!` with a drop-in replacement, adding a colorful diff.

## Usage

When writing tests in Rust, you'll probably use `assert_eq!(a, b)` *a lot*.

If such a test fails, it will present all the details of `a` and `b`.
But you have to spot the differences yourself, which is not always straightforward,
like here:

Wouldn't that task be *much* easier with a colorful diff?

Yep — and you only need **one line of code** to make it happen:

```
use ;
```
```
// 1. add the `pretty_assertions` dependency to `Cargo.toml`.
// 2. insert this line at the top of each module, as needed
use ;
```
## Semantic Versioning

The exact output of assertions is **not guaranteed** to be consistent over time, and may change between minor versions.
The output of this crate is designed to be read by a human. It is not suitable for exact comparison, for example in snapshot testing.

This crate adheres to semantic versioning for publically exported crate items, **except** the `private` module, which may change between any version.

## Tip

Specify it as [ [dev-dependencies]](http://doc.crates.io/specifying-dependencies.html#development-dependencies)
and it will only be used for compiling tests, examples, and benchmarks.
This way the compile time of

`cargo build` won't be affected!Also add `#[cfg(test)]` to your `use` statements, like this:

```
use ;
```
## Notes

- Since `Rust 2018`edition, you need to declare`use pretty_assertions::{assert_eq, assert_ne};`per module. Before you would write`#[macro_use] extern crate pretty_assertions;`.
- The replacement is only effective in your own crate, not in other libraries you include.
- `assert_ne`is also switched to multi-line presentation, but does- *not*show a diff.
- Under Windows, the terminal state is modified to properly handle VT100 escape sequences, which may break display for certain use cases.
- The minimum supported rust version (MSRV) is 1.35.0

`no_std` support

For `no_std` support, disable the `std` feature and enable the `alloc` feature:

```
# Cargo.toml
 = { = "...",  = false,  = ["alloc"] }
```

# libtest-mimic 0.8.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/libtest-mimic/0.8.1

# libtest-mimic

Write your own test harness that looks and behaves like the built-in test harness (used by `rustc --test`)!

This is a simple and small testing framework that mimics the original `libtest`.
That means: all output looks pretty much like `cargo test` and most CLI arguments are understood and used.
With that plumbing work out of the way, your test runner can focus on the actual testing.

See [ the documentation](https://docs.rs/libtest-mimic) or

[the](https://docs.rs/examples)for more information.

# libtest-mimic 0.4.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/libtest-mimic/0.4.1

# libtest-mimic

Write your own test harness that looks and behaves like the built-in test harness (used by `rustc --test`)! (MSRV 1.56)

This is a simple and small testing framework that mimics the original `libtest` (used by `rustc --test`). That means: all output looks pretty much like `cargo test` and most CLI arguments are understood and used. With that plumbing work out of the way, your test runner can concentrate on the actual testing.

**See it in action** (with the `tidy` example):

# Example

```
extern crate libtest_mimic;
use ;
// Parse command line arguments
let args = from_args;
// Create a list of tests (in this case: three dummy tests)
let tests = vec!;
// Run all tests and exit the application appropriatly (in this case, the
// test runner is a dummy runner which does nothing and says that all s
// passed).
run_tests.exit;
```
For more examples, see [ examples/](https://github.com/LukasKalbertodt/libtest-mimic/tree/master/examples).

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/libtest-mimic/0.2.0

# libtest-mimic

Write your own test harness that looks and behaves like the built-in test harness (used by `rustc --test`)!

This is a simple and small testing framework that mimics the original `libtest` (used by `rustc --test`). That means: all output looks pretty much like `cargo test` and most CLI arguments are understood and used. With that plumbing work out of the way, your test runner can concentrate on the actual testing.

**See it in action** (with the `tidy` example):

# Example

```
extern crate libtest_mimic;
use ;
// Parse command line arguments
let args = from_args;
// Create a list of tests (in this case: three dummy tests)
let tests = vec!;
// Run all tests and exit the application appropriatly (in this case, the
// test runner is a dummy runner which does nothing and says that all s
// passed).
run_tests.exit;
```
For more examples, see [ examples/](https://github.com/LukasKalbertodt/libtest-mimic/tree/master/examples).

# libtest_mimic - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/libtest-mimic

## Expand description

Write your own tests and benchmarks that look and behave like built-in tests!

This is a simple and small test harness that mimics the original `libtest`
(used by `cargo test`/`rustc --test`). That means: all output looks pretty
much like `cargo test` and most CLI arguments are understood and used. With
that plumbing work out of the way, your test runner can focus on the actual
testing.

For a small real world example, see [ examples/tidy.rs](https://github.com/LukasKalbertodt/libtest-mimic/blob/master/examples/tidy.rs).

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

To use this, you most likely want to add a manual `[[test]]` section to
`Cargo.toml` and set `harness = false`. For example:

```
[[test]]
name = "mytest"
path = "tests/mytest.rs"
harness = false
```
And in `tests/mytest.rs` you would call [ run](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html) in the

`main` function:```
use libtest_mimic::{Arguments, Trial};
// Parse command line arguments
let args = Arguments::from_args();
// Create a list of tests and/or benchmarks (in this case: two dummy tests).
let tests = vec![
    Trial::test("succeeding_test", move || Ok(())),
    Trial::test("failing_test", move || Err("Woops".into())),
];
// Run all tests and exit the application appropriatly.
libtest_mimic::run(&args, tests).exit();
```
Instead of returning `Ok` or `Err` directly, you want to actually perform
your tests, of course. See [ Trial::test](https://docs.rs/struct.Trial.html#method.test) for more information on how to
define a test. You can of course list all your tests manually. But in many
cases it is useful to generate one test per file in a directory, for
example.

You can then run `cargo test --test mytest` to run it. To see the CLI
arguments supported by this crate, run `cargo test --test mytest -- -h`.

[§](https://docs.rs#known-limitations-and-differences-to-the-official-test-harness)Known limitations and differences to the official test harness

`libtest-mimic` works on a best-effort basis: it tries to be as close to
`libtest` as possible, but there are differences for a variety of reasons.
For example, some rarely used features might not be implemented, some
features are extremely difficult to implement, and removing minor,
unimportant differences is just not worth the hassle.

Some of the notable differences:

- Output capture and `--nocapture`: simply not supported. The official`libtest`uses internal`std`functions to temporarily redirect output.`libtest-mimic`cannot use those. See[this issue](https://github.com/LukasKalbertodt/libtest-mimic/issues/9)for more information.
- `--format=junit`
- Also see [#13](https://github.com/LukasKalbertodt/libtest-mimic/issues/13)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Arguments](https://docs.rs/struct.Arguments.html)
- Command line arguments.
- [Conclusion](https://docs.rs/struct.Conclusion.html)
- Contains information about the entire test run. Is returned by`run`
- [Failed](https://docs.rs/struct.Failed.html)
- Indicates that a test/benchmark has failed. Optionally carries a message.
- [Measurement](https://docs.rs/struct.Measurement.html)
- Output of a benchmark.
- [Trial](https://docs.rs/struct.Trial.html)
- A single test or benchmark.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorSetting.html)- Setting
- Possible values for the `--color`option.
- [Completion](https://docs.rs/enum.Completion.html)
- A representation of whether a test ran to completion or was ignored during its runtime.
- [Format](https://docs.rs/enum.FormatSetting.html)- Setting
- Possible values for the `--format`option.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [run](https://docs.rs/fn.run.html)
- Runs all given trials (tests & benchmarks).

# anstream 1.0.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/anstream/1.0.0

# anstream

A simple cross platform library for writing colored text to a terminal.

*A portmanteau of "ansi stream"*

Specialized `stdout` and `stderr` that accept ANSI escape codes and adapt them
based on the terminal's capabilities.

`anstream::adapter::strip_str` may also be of interest on its own for low
overhead stripping of ANSI escape codes.

# anstyle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/anstyle/^1.0.0/

## Expand description

ANSI Text Styling

*A portmanteau of “ansi style”*

`anstyle` provides core types describing [ANSI styling escape
codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code) for interoperability
between crates.

Example use cases:

- An argument parser allowing callers to define the colors used in the help-output without putting the text formatting crate in the public API
- A style description parser that can work with any text formatting crate

Priorities:

- API stability
- Low compile-time and binary-size overhead
- `const`friendly API for callers to statically define their stylesheet

For integration with text styling crate, see:

User-styling parsers:

- [anstyle-git](https://docs.rs/anstyle-git): Parse Git style descriptions
- [anstyle-ls](https://docs.rs/anstyle-ls): Parse- `LS_COLORS`style descriptions

Convert to other formats

- [anstream](https://docs.rs/anstream): A simple cross platform library for writing colored text to a terminal
- [anstyle-roff](https://docs.rs/anstyle-roff): For converting to ROFF
- [anstyle-syntect](https://docs.rs/anstyle-syntect): For working with syntax highlighting

Utilities

- [anstyle-lossy](https://docs.rs/anstyle-lossy): Convert between- `anstyle::Color`types
- [anstyle-parse](https://docs.rs/anstyle-parse): Parsing ANSI Style Escapes
- [anstyle-wincon](https://docs.rs/anstyle-wincon): Styling legacy Microsoft terminals

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

The core type is [ Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html):

`let style = anstyle::Style::new().bold();`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# anstyle_parse - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/anstyle-parse/^1.0.0/

## Expand description

Parser for implementing virtual terminal emulators

[ Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html) is implemented according to

[Paul Williams’ ANSI parser state machine](https://vt100.net/emu/dec_ansi_parser). The state machine doesn’t assign meaning to the parsed data and is thus not itself sufficient for writing a terminal emulator. Instead, it is expected that an implementation of

[is provided which does something useful with the parsed data. The](https://docs.rs/trait.Perform.html)

`Perform`[handles the book keeping, and the](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html)

`Parser`[gets to simply handle actions.](https://docs.rs/trait.Perform.html)

`Perform`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

For an example of using the [ Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html) please see the examples folder. The example included
there simply logs all the actions

[does. One quick thing to see it in action is to pipe](https://docs.rs/trait.Perform.html)

`Perform``vim` into it```
cargo build --release --example parselog
vim | target/release/examples/parselog
```
Just type `:q` to exit.

[§](https://docs.rs#differences-from-original-state-machine-description)Differences from original state machine description

- UTF-8 Support for Input
- OSC Strings can be terminated by 0x07
- Only supports 7-bit codes. Some 8-bit codes are still supported, but they no longer work in all states.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [state](https://docs.rs/state/index.html)
- ANSI escape code parsing state machine

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ascii](https://docs.rs/struct.AsciiParser.html)- Parser
- Only allow parsing 7-bit ASCII
- [Params](https://docs.rs/struct.Params.html)
- [Params](https://docs.rs/struct.ParamsIter.html)- Iter
- Immutable subparameter iterator.
- [Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html)
- Parser for raw *VTE*protocol which delegates actions to a`Perform`
- [Utf8](https://docs.rs/struct.Utf8Parser.html)- Parser - `utf8`
- Allow parsing UTF-8

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Char](https://docs.rs/trait.CharAccumulator.html)- Accumulator
- Build a `char`out of bytes
- [Perform](https://docs.rs/trait.Perform.html)
- Performs actions requested by the `Parser`

## Type Aliases[§](https://docs.rs#types)

- [Default](https://docs.rs/type.DefaultCharAccumulator.html)- Char - Accumulator - `utf8`

# lexopt - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lexopt/^0.3.1/

## Expand description

A pathologically simple command line argument parser.

Most argument parsers are declarative: you tell them what to parse, and they do it.

This one provides you with a stream of options and values and lets you figure out the rest.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
struct Args {
    thing: String,
    number: u32,
    shout: bool,
}
fn parse_args() -> Result<Args, lexopt::Error> {
    use lexopt::prelude::*;
    let mut thing = None;
    let mut number = 1;
    let mut shout = false;
    let mut parser = lexopt::Parser::from_env();
    while let Some(arg) = parser.next()? {
        match arg {
            Short('n') | Long("number") => {
                number = parser.value()?.parse()?;
            }
            Long("shout") => {
                shout = true;
            }
            Value(val) if thing.is_none() => {
                thing = Some(val.string()?);
            }
            Long("help") => {
                println!("Usage: hello [-n|--number=NUM] [--shout] THING");
                std::process::exit(0);
            }
            _ => return Err(arg.unexpected()),
        }
    }
    Ok(Args {
        thing: thing.ok_or("missing argument THING")?,
        number,
        shout,
    })
}
fn main() -> Result<(), lexopt::Error> {
    let args = parse_args()?;
    let mut message = format!("Hello {}", args.thing);
    if args.shout {
        message = message.to_uppercase();
    }
    for _ in 0..args.number {
        println!("{}", message);
    }
    Ok(())
}
```
Let’s walk through this:

- We start parsing with `Parser::from_env`
- We call `parser.next()`
- We match on arguments. `Short``Long`
- To get the value that belongs to an option (like `10`in`-n 10`) we call`parser.value()`- This returns a standard `OsString`
- For convenience, `use lexopt::prelude::*``.parse()``str::parse`
- Calling `parser.value()`is how we tell`Parser`that`-n`takes a value at all.

- This returns a standard
- `Value`indicates a free-standing argument.- `if thing.is_none()`is a useful pattern for positional arguments. If we already found- `thing`we pass it on to another case.
- It also contains an `OsString`.- The `.string()``String`.

- The

- If we don’t know what to do with an argument we use `return Err(arg.unexpected())`
- Strings can be promoted to errors for custom error messages.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- A small prelude for processing arguments.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Parser](https://docs.rs/struct.Parser.html)
- A parser for command line arguments.
- [RawArgs](https://docs.rs/struct.RawArgs.html)
- An iterator for the remaining raw arguments, returned by `Parser::raw_args`
- [Values](https://docs.rs/struct.ValuesIter.html)- Iter
- An iterator for multiple option-arguments, returned by `Parser::values`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Arg](https://docs.rs/enum.Arg.html)
- A command line argument found by `Parser`
- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- An error during argument parsing.

# owo_colors - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/owo-colors/^4.0.0/

## Expand description

This crate provides [ OwoColorize](https://docs.rs/trait.OwoColorize.html), an extension trait for colorizing a
given type.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use owo_colors::OwoColorize;
// Foreground colors
println!("My number is {:#x}!", 10.green());
// Background colors
println!("My number is not {}!", 4.on_red());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#generically-color)Generically color

```
use owo_colors::OwoColorize;
use owo_colors::colors::*;
// Generically color
println!("My number might be {}!", 4.fg::<Black>().bg::<Yellow>());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#stylize)Stylize

```
use owo_colors::OwoColorize;
println!("{}", "strikethrough".strikethrough());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#only-style-on-supported-terminals)Only Style on Supported Terminals

```
use owo_colors::{OwoColorize, Stream::Stdout};
println!(
    "{}",
    "colored blue if a supported terminal"
        .if_supports_color(Stdout, |text| text.bright_blue())
);
```
Supports `NO_COLOR`/`FORCE_COLOR` environment variables, checks if it’s a tty, checks
if it’s running in CI (and thus likely supports color), and checks which terminal is being
used. (Note: requires `supports-colors` feature)

[§](https://docs.rs#style-objects)Style Objects

owo-colors also features the ability to create a [ Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html) object and use it to
apply the same set of colors/effects to any number of things to display.

```
use owo_colors::{OwoColorize, Style};
let my_style = Style::new()
    .red()
    .on_white()
    .strikethrough();
let text = "red text, white background, struck through";
println!("{}", text.style(my_style));
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [colored](https://docs.rs/colored/index.html)
- Module for drop-in `colored``colored`
- [colors](https://docs.rs/colors/index.html)
- Color types for used for being generic over the color
- [styles](https://docs.rs/styles/index.html)
- Different display styles (strikethrough, bold, etc.)

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BgColor](https://docs.rs/struct.BgColorDisplay.html)- Display
- Transparent wrapper around a type which implements all the formatters the wrapped type does,
with the addition of changing the background color. Recommended to be constructed using
`OwoColorize`
- [BgDyn](https://docs.rs/struct.BgDynColorDisplay.html)- Color - Display
- Wrapper around a type which implements all the formatters the wrapped type does, with the addition of changing the background color. Is not recommended unless compile-time coloring is not an option.
- [Combo](https://docs.rs/struct.ComboColorDisplay.html)- Color - Display
- A wrapper type which applies both a foreground and background color
- [Combo](https://docs.rs/struct.ComboDynColorDisplay.html)- DynColor - Display
- Wrapper around a type which implements all the formatters the wrapped type does, with the addition of changing the foreground and background color.
- [FgColor](https://docs.rs/struct.FgColorDisplay.html)- Display
- Transparent wrapper around a type which implements all the formatters the wrapped type does,
with the addition of changing the foreground color. Recommended to be constructed using
`OwoColorize`
- [FgDyn](https://docs.rs/struct.FgDynColorDisplay.html)- Color - Display
- Wrapper around a type which implements all the formatters the wrapped type does, with the addition of changing the foreground color. Is not recommended unless compile-time coloring is not an option.
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/struct.ParseColorError.html)- Color - Error
- An error for when the color can not be parsed from a string at runtime
- [Rgb](https://docs.rs/struct.Rgb.html)
- Available RGB colors for use with `OwoColorize::color``OwoColorize::on_color`

# strip_ansi_escapes - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/strip-ansi-escapes/^0.2.1/

## Expand description

A crate for stripping ANSI escape sequences from byte sequences.

This can be used to take output from a program that includes escape sequences and write it somewhere that does not easily support them, such as a log file.

The simplest interface provided is the [ strip](https://docs.rs/fn.strip.html) function, which takes a byte slice and returns
a

`Vec` of bytes with escape sequences removed. For writing bytes directly to a writer, you
may prefer using the [struct, which implements](https://docs.rs/struct.Writer.html)

`Writer``Write` and strips escape sequences
as they are written.[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use std::io::{self, Write};
let bytes_with_colors = b"\x1b[32mfoo\x1b[m bar";
let plain_bytes = strip_ansi_escapes::strip(&bytes_with_colors);
io::stdout().write_all(&plain_bytes)?;
```
## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Writer](https://docs.rs/struct.Writer.html)
- `Writer`wraps an underlying type that implements- `Write`, stripping ANSI escape sequences from bytes written to it before passing them to the underlying writer.

# anstream - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/anstream/1.0.0/target-redirect/anstream/

## Expand description

**Auto-adapting **

`stdout` / `stderr` streams*A portmanteau of “ansi stream”*

[ AutoStream](https://docs.rs/struct.AutoStream.html) always accepts

[ANSI escape codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code),

[adapting to the user’s terminal’s capabilities](https://docs.rs/struct.AutoStream.html).

Benefits

- Allows the caller to not be concerned with the terminal’s capabilities
- Semver safe way of passing styled text between crates as ANSI escape codes offer more compatibility than most crate APIs.

Available styling crates:

- [anstyle](https://docs.rs/anstyle)for minimal runtime styling, designed to go in public APIs
- [owo-colors](https://docs.rs/owo-colors)for feature-rich runtime styling
- [color-print](https://docs.rs/color-print)for feature-rich compile-time styling

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use anstream::println;
use owo_colors::OwoColorize as _;
// Foreground colors
println!("My number is {:#x}!", 10.green());
// Background colors
println!("My number is not {}!", 4.on_red());
```
And this will correctly handle piping to a file, etc

# AutoStream in anstream - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/anstream/^1/struct.AutoStream.html

`pub struct AutoStream<S: `[RawStream](https://docs.rs/stream/trait.RawStream.html)> { /* private fields */ }## Expand description

[ std::io::Write](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html) that adapts ANSI escape codes to the underlying

`Write`s capabilitiesThis includes

- Stripping colors for non-terminals
- Respecting env variables like [NO_COLOR](https://no-color.org/)or[CLICOLOR](https://bixense.com/clicolors/)
- *(windows)*Falling back to the wincon API where- [ENABLE_VIRTUAL_TERMINAL_PROCESSING](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/console/console-virtual-terminal-sequences#output-sequences)is unsupported

You can customize auto-detection by calling into
[anstyle_query](https://docs.rs/anstyle-query/latest/anstyle_query/)
to get a [ ColorChoice](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorChoice.html) and then calling [

`AutoStream::new(stream, choice)`].## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/anstream/auto.rs.html#62-72)

#### pub fn [new](https://docs.rs#method.new)(raw: S, choice: [ColorChoice](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorChoice.html)) -> Self

Runtime control over styling behavior

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
// Like `AutoStream::choice` but without `NO_COLOR`, `CLICOLOR_FORCE`, `CI`
fn choice(raw: &dyn anstream::stream::RawStream) -> anstream::ColorChoice {
    let choice = anstream::ColorChoice::global();
    if choice == anstream::ColorChoice::Auto {
        if raw.is_terminal() && anstyle_query::term_supports_color() {
            anstream::ColorChoice::Always
        } else {
            anstream::ColorChoice::Never
        }
    } else {
        choice
    }
}
let stream = std::io::stdout();
let choice = choice(&stream);
let auto = anstream::AutoStream::new(stream, choice);
```
Auto-adapt for the stream’s capabilities

# anstyle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/anstyle

## Expand description

ANSI Text Styling

*A portmanteau of “ansi style”*

`anstyle` provides core types describing [ANSI styling escape
codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code) for interoperability
between crates.

Example use cases:

- An argument parser allowing callers to define the colors used in the help-output without putting the text formatting crate in the public API
- A style description parser that can work with any text formatting crate

Priorities:

- API stability
- Low compile-time and binary-size overhead
- `const`friendly API for callers to statically define their stylesheet

For integration with text styling crate, see:

User-styling parsers:

- [anstyle-git](https://docs.rs/anstyle-git): Parse Git style descriptions
- [anstyle-ls](https://docs.rs/anstyle-ls): Parse- `LS_COLORS`style descriptions

Convert to other formats

- [anstream](https://docs.rs/anstream): A simple cross platform library for writing colored text to a terminal
- [anstyle-roff](https://docs.rs/anstyle-roff): For converting to ROFF
- [anstyle-syntect](https://docs.rs/anstyle-syntect): For working with syntax highlighting

Utilities

- [anstyle-lossy](https://docs.rs/anstyle-lossy): Convert between- `anstyle::Color`types
- [anstyle-parse](https://docs.rs/anstyle-parse): Parsing ANSI Style Escapes
- [anstyle-wincon](https://docs.rs/anstyle-wincon): Styling legacy Microsoft terminals

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

The core type is [ Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html):

`let style = anstyle::Style::new().bold();`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Ansi256](https://docs.rs/struct.Ansi256Color.html)- Color
- 256 (8-bit) color support
- [Effect](https://docs.rs/struct.EffectIter.html)- Iter
- Enumerate each enabled value in `Effects`
- [Effects](https://docs.rs/struct.Effects.html)
- A set of text effects
- [Reset](https://docs.rs/struct.Reset.html)
- Reset terminal formatting
- [RgbColor](https://docs.rs/struct.RgbColor.html)
- 24-bit ANSI RGB color codes
- [Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html)
- ANSI Text styling

# owo_colors - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/owo-colors

## Expand description

This crate provides [ OwoColorize](https://docs.rs/trait.OwoColorize.html), an extension trait for colorizing a
given type.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use owo_colors::OwoColorize;
// Foreground colors
println!("My number is {:#x}!", 10.green());
// Background colors
println!("My number is not {}!", 4.on_red());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#generically-color)Generically color

```
use owo_colors::OwoColorize;
use owo_colors::colors::*;
// Generically color
println!("My number might be {}!", 4.fg::<Black>().bg::<Yellow>());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#stylize)Stylize

```
use owo_colors::OwoColorize;
println!("{}", "strikethrough".strikethrough());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#only-style-on-supported-terminals)Only Style on Supported Terminals

```
use owo_colors::{OwoColorize, Stream::Stdout};
println!(
    "{}",
    "colored blue if a supported terminal"
        .if_supports_color(Stdout, |text| text.bright_blue())
);
```
Supports `NO_COLOR`/`FORCE_COLOR` environment variables, checks if it’s a tty, checks
if it’s running in CI (and thus likely supports color), and checks which terminal is being
used. (Note: requires `supports-colors` feature)

[§](https://docs.rs#style-objects)Style Objects

owo-colors also features the ability to create a [ Style](https://docs.rs/struct.Style.html) object and use it to
apply the same set of colors/effects to any number of things to display.

```
use owo_colors::{OwoColorize, Style};
let my_style = Style::new()
    .red()
    .on_white()
    .strikethrough();
let text = "red text, white background, struck through";
println!("{}", text.style(my_style));
```
## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [colored](https://docs.rs/colored/index.html)
- Module for drop-in `colored``colored`

# color_print - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/color-print

## Expand description

Colorize and stylize strings for terminal at compile-time, by using an HTML-like syntax.

This library provides the following macros:

- `cformat!(<FORMAT_STRING> [, ARGS...])`
- `cprint!(<FORMAT_STRING> [, ARGS...])`
- `cprintln!(<FORMAT_STRING> [, ARGS...])`
- `ceprint!(<FORMAT_STRING> [, ARGS...])`
- `ceprintln!(<FORMAT_STRING> [, ARGS...])`
- `cwrite!(f, <FORMAT_STRING> [, ARGS...])`
- `cwriteln!(f, <FORMAT_STRING> [, ARGS...])`
- `cstr!(<FORMAT_STRING>)`
- `untagged!(<FORMAT_STRING>)`

The macros have the same syntax as their corresponding [ std](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/index.html) variants:

- `cformat!()`- `format!()`
- `cprint!()`- `print!()`
- `cprintln!()`- `println!()`
- `ceprint!()`- `eprint!()`
- `ceprintln!()`- `eprintln!()`
- `cwrite!()`- `write!()`
- `cwriteln!()`- `writeln!()`

But they accept an additional syntax inside the format string: HTML-like tags which add ANSI colors/styles at compile-time.

[ cstr!()](https://docs.rs/macro.cstr.html) only transforms the given string literal into another string literal, without
formatting anything else than the colors tag.

[ untagged!()](https://docs.rs/macro.untagged.html) removes all the tags found in the given string literal.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-does-it-do-)What does it do ?

By default, the provided macros will replace the tags found in the format string by ANSI hexadecimal escape codes. E.g.:

```
cprintln!("HELLO <green>WORLD</green>");
cprintln!("HELLO <green>WORLD</>"); // Alternative, shorter syntax
```
will be replaced by:

`println!("HELLO \u{1b}[31mWORLD\u{1b}[39m")`*Note*: it is possible to change this behaviour by activating the feature `terminfo`. Then it
will question the `terminfo` database at runtime in order to know which sequence to write for
each kind of styling/colorizing (see below for more detail).

[§](https://docs.rs#proscons-of-this-crate)Pros/cons of this crate

[§](https://docs.rs#pros)Pros

- Styling is processed at compile-time, so the runtime payload is  inexistant (unless the
feature `terminfo`is activated);
- Nested tags are well handled, e.g. `"<green>...<blue>...</blue>...</green>"`;
- Some optimizations are performed to avoid redundant ANSI sequences, because these optimizations can be done at compile-time without impacting the runtime;
- Almost every tag has a short name, so colorizing can be done quickly: `"my <b>blue</> word"`;
- Each provided macro can be used exactly in the same way as the standard `format!`-like macros; e.g., positional arguments and named arguments can be used as usual;
- Supports 16, 256 and 16M colors;
- Fine-grained error handling (errors will be given at compile-time).

[§](https://docs.rs#cons)Cons

- Not compatible with non-ANSI terminals.

[§](https://docs.rs#introduction)Introduction

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-example)Basic example

```
use color_print::cprintln;
cprintln!("Hello <green>world</green>!");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#closing-a-tag-more-simply-the--tag)Closing a tag more simply: the `</>` tag

Basically, tags must be closed by giving *exactly* the same colors/styles as their matching
open tag (with a slash `/` at the beginning), e.g: `<blue,bold>...</blue,bold>`. But it can be
tedious!

So, it is also possible to close the last open tag simply with `</>`:

`cprintln!("Hello <green>world</>!");`[§](https://docs.rs#combining-colors-and-styles)Combining colors and styles

Multiple styles and colors can be combined into a single tag by separating them with the `,`
comma character:

```
cprintln!("This a <green,bold>green and bold text</green,bold>.");
// The same, but closing with the </> tag:
cprintln!("This a <green,bold>green and bold text</>.");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#nesting-tags)Nesting tags

Any tag can be nested with any other.

*Note*: The closing tags must match correctly (following the basic rules of nesting for HTML
tags), but it can always be simplified by using the tag `</>`.

Example of nested tags:

```
cprintln!("<green>This is green, <bold>then green and bold</bold>, then green again</green>");
cprintln!("<green>This is green, <bold>then green and bold</>, then green again</>");
// Colors can be nested as well:
cprintln!("<green>This is green, <blue>then blue</blue>, then green again</green>");
cprintln!("<green>This is green, <blue>then blue</>, then green again</>");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#unclosed-tags-are-automatically-closed-at-the-end-of-the-format-string)Unclosed tags are automatically closed at the end of the format string

Tags which have not been closed manually will be closed automatically, which means that the ANSI sequences needed to go back to the original state will be added:

```
// The two following lines are strictly equivalent:
cprintln!("<green><bold>Hello");
cprintln!("<green><bold>Hello</></>");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#how-to-display-the-chars--and--verbatim)How to display the chars `<` and `>` verbatim

As for `{` and `}` in standard format strings, the chars `<` and `>` have to be doubled in
order to display them verbatim:

`cprintln!("This is an angle bracket character: <<, and here is another one: >>");`[§](https://docs.rs#optimization-no-redundant-ansi-codes)Optimization: no redundant ANSI codes

The expanded format string will only contain the *needed* ANSI codes. This is done by making a
diff of the different style attributes, each time a tag is encountered, instead of mechanically
adding the ANSI codes.

E.g., several nested `<bold>` tags will only produce one bold ANSI sequence:

`cprintln!("<bold><bold> A <bold,blue> B </> C </></>")`will be replaced by:

```
println!("\u{1b}[1m A \u{1b}[34m B \u{1b}[39m C \u{1b}[22m")
//        ^-------^   ^--------^   ^--------^   ^--------^
//          bold         blue         color        bold
//                                    reset        reset
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-feature-terminfo)The feature `terminfo`

Instead of inserting ANSI sequences directly into the format string, it is possible to activate
the feature `terminfo`: this will add the format sequences at runtime, by consulting the
`terminfo` database.

This has one pro and several cons:

[§](https://docs.rs#pros-1)Pros

- This adds a level of compatibility for some terminals.

[§](https://docs.rs#cons-1)Cons

- This adds a little runtime payload;
- This adds two dependencies: `lazy_static``terminfo`
- The styles `<strike>`and`<conceal>`are not handled;
- With `terminfo`, many styles are not resettable individually, which implies longer format sequences for the same result;
- For now, the provided macros can only be used in one thread.

[§](https://docs.rs#naming-rules-of-the-tags)Naming rules of the tags:

Each tag has at least a **long name**, like `<magenta>` or `<underline>`.

The tags directly relative to *colors* (like `<red>`, `<bg:blue>`, `<bg:bright-green>`…, as
opposed to *style* tags like `<bold>`, `<italics>`…) have some common naming rules:

- Each tag has four variants:
- `<mycolor>`: the normal, foreground color;
- `<bright-mycolor>`or- `<mycolor!>`: the bright, foreground color;
- `<bg:mycolor>`,- `<MYCOLOR>`: the normal, background color;
- `<bg:bright-mycolor>`,- `<bg:mycolor!>`,- `<BRIGHT-MYCOLOR>`or- `<MYCOLOR!>`: the bright, background color;

- Each tag has a *shortcut*, with a base letter for each color; example with the`x`letter:- `<x>`: the normal, foreground color;
- `<x!>`: the bright, foreground color;
- `<bg:x>`,- `<X>`: the normal, background color;
- `<bg:x!>`,- `<X!>`: the bright, background color;

- Each color’s shortcut letter is simply the **first letter of its name**(excepted for`<k>`which is the shortcut for`<black>`), e.g.`<y>`is the shortcut for`<yellow>`;
- Each color’s tag which is uppercase is a **background color**;
- Each tag which has a trailing exclamation point `!`is a**bright color**;

[§](https://docs.rs#list-of-accepted-tags)List of accepted tags:

The two first columns show which styles are supported, respectively with the default crate
features (ANSI column), and with the feature `terminfo` being activated.

**crate feature**only.

`auto`## Expand description

Prints to [ stderr](https://docs.rs/fn.stderr.html).

Equivalent to the [ print!](https://docs.rs/macro.print.html) macro, except that output goes to

`stderr` instead of `stdout`. See [for example usage.](https://docs.rs/macro.print.html)

`print!`Use `eprint!` only for error and progress messages. Use `print!`

**NOTE:** Not all `eprint!` calls will be captured in tests like `std::eprint!`

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Writing to non-blocking stdout can cause an error, which will lead this macro to panic.

```

# panic in anstream - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/anstream/^1/macro.panic.html

```
macro_rules! panic {
    () => { ... };
    ($($arg:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
**crate feature**only.

`auto`## Expand description

Panics the current thread.

This allows a program to terminate immediately and provide feedback to the caller of the program.

This macro is the perfect way to assert conditions in example code and in
tests. `panic!` is closely tied with the `unwrap` method of both
[ Option](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#method.unwrap) and

[enums. Both implementations call](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#method.unwrap)

`Result``panic!` when they are set to [or](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None)

`None`[variants.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)

`Err`When using `panic!()` you can specify a string payload, that is built using
the [ format!](https://docs.rs/std/macro.format.html) syntax. That payload is used when injecting the panic into
the calling Rust thread, causing the thread to panic entirely.

The behavior of the default `std` hook, i.e. the code that runs directly
after the panic is invoked, is to print the message payload to
`stderr` along with the file/line/column information of the `panic!()`
call. You can override the panic hook using [ std::panic::set_hook()](https://docs.rs/std/panic/fn.set_hook.html).
Inside the hook a panic can be accessed as a

`&dyn Any + Send`,
which contains either a `&str` or `String` for regular `panic!()` invocations.
To panic with a value of another other type, [can be used.](https://docs.rs/std/panic/fn.panic_any.html)

`panic_any`See also the macro [ compile_error!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/macro.compile_error.html), for raising errors during compilation.

[§](https://docs.rs#when-to-use-panic-vs-result)When to use `panic!` vs `Result`

The Rust language provides two complementary systems for constructing /
representing, reporting, propagating, reacting to, and discarding errors. These
responsibilities are collectively known as “error handling.” `panic!` and
`Result` are similar in that they are each the primary interface of their
respective error handling systems; however, the meaning these interfaces attach
to their errors and the responsibilities they fulfill within their respective
error handling systems differ.

The `panic!` macro is used to construct errors that represent a bug that has
been detected in your program. With `panic!` you provide a message that
describes the bug and the language then constructs an error with that message,
reports it, and propagates it for you.

`Result` on the other hand is used to wrap other types that represent either
the successful result of some computation, `Ok(T)`, or error types that
represent an anticipated runtime failure mode of that computation, `Err(E)`.
`Result` is used alongside user defined types which represent the various
anticipated runtime failure modes that the associated computation could
encounter. `Result` must be propagated manually, often with the help of the
`?` operator and `Try` trait, and they must be reported manually, often with
the help of the `Error` trait.

For more detailed information about error handling check out the [book](https://docs.rs/book/ch09-00-error-handling.html) or the
[ std::result](https://docs.rs/std/result/index.html) module docs.

[§](https://docs.rs#current-implementation)Current implementation

If the main thread panics it will terminate all your threads and end your
program with code `101`.

# print in anstream - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/anstream/^1/macro.print.html

```
macro_rules! print {
    ($($arg:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
**crate feature**only.

`auto`## Expand description

Prints to [ stdout](https://docs.rs/fn.stdout.html).

Equivalent to the [ println!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/macro.println.html) macro except that a newline is not printed at
the end of the message.

Note that stdout is frequently line-buffered by default so it may be
necessary to use [ std::io::Write::flush()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/trait.Write.html#tymethod.flush) to ensure the output is emitted
immediately.

**NOTE:** The `print!` macro will lock the standard output on each call. If you call
`print!` within a hot loop, this behavior may be the bottleneck of the loop.
To avoid this, lock stdout with [ AutoStream::lock](https://docs.rs/struct.AutoStream.html#method.lock):

```
use std::io::Write as _;
let mut lock = anstream::stdout().lock();
write!(lock, "hello world").unwrap();
```
Use `print!` only for the primary output of your program. Use
[ eprint!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/macro.eprint.html) instead to print error and progress messages.

**NOTE:** Not all `print!` calls will be captured in tests like `std::print!`

- Capturing will automatically be activated in test binaries
- Otherwise, only when the `test`feature is enabled

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if writing to `stdout` fails for any reason **except** broken pipe.

Writing to non-blocking stdout can cause an error, which will lead this macro to panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use std::io::Write as _;
use anstream::print;
use anstream::stdout;
print!("this ");
print!("will ");
print!("be ");
print!("on ");
print!("the ");
print!("same ");
print!("line ");
stdout().flush().unwrap();
print!("this string has a newline, why not choose println! instead?\n");
stdout().flush().unwrap();
```

# println in anstream - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/anstream/^1/macro.println.html

```
macro_rules! println {
    () => { ... };
    ($($arg:tt)*) => { ... };
}
```
**crate feature**only.

`auto`## Expand description

Prints to [ stdout](https://docs.rs/fn.stdout.html), with a newline.

On all platforms, the newline is the LINE FEED character (`\n`/`U+000A`) alone
(no additional CARRIAGE RETURN (`\r`/`U+000D`)).

This macro uses the same syntax as [ format!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/macro.format.html), but writes to the standard output instead.
See

[for more information.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/fmt/index.html)

`std::fmt`**NOTE:** The `println!` macro will lock the standard output on each call. If you call
`println!` within a hot loop, this behavior may be the bottleneck of the loop.
To avoid this, lock stdout with [ AutoStream::lock](https://docs.rs/struct.AutoStream.html#method.lock):

```
use std::io::Write as _;
let mut lock = anstream::stdout().lock();
writeln!(lock, "hello world").unwrap();
```
Use `println!` only for the primary output of your program. Use
[ eprintln!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/macro.eprintln.html) instead to print error and progress messages.

**NOTE:** Not all `println!` calls will be captured in tests like `std::println!`

- Capturing will automatically be activated in test binaries
- Otherwise, only when the `test`feature is enabled

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if writing to `stdout` fails for any reason **except** broken pipe.

Writing to non-blocking stdout can cause an error, which will lead this macro to panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use anstream::println;
println!(); // prints just a newline
println!("hello there!");
println!("format {} arguments", "some");
let local_variable = "some";
println!("format {local_variable} arguments");
```

# ColorChoice in anstream - Rust

```
pub enum ColorChoice {
    Auto,
    AlwaysAnsi,
    Always,
    Never,
}
```
## Expand description

Selection for overriding color output Selection for overriding color output

## Variants[§](https://docs.rs#variants)

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Auto)

### Auto

Use colors if the output device appears to support them

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.AlwaysAnsi)

### AlwaysAnsi

Like `Always`, except it never tries to use anything other than emitting ANSI
color codes.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Always)

### Always

Try very hard to emit colors.

This includes emitting ANSI colors on Windows if the console API is unavailable.

[§](https://docs.rs#variant.Never)

### Never

Never emit colors.

# anstyle

ANSI text styling

*A portmanteau of "ansi style"*

`anstyle` provides core types describing [ANSI styling escape
codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code) for interoperability
between crates.  For example, this would allow a crate to provide an API for
customizing the colors used without putting the underlying text styling crate
in the API.

For integration with your text styling crate, see:

# snapbox - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/snapbox/^0.6.23/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#snapshot-testing-toolbox)Snapshot testing toolbox

When you have to treat your tests like pets, instead of

[cattle](https://docs.rs/trycmd)

`snapbox` is a snapshot-testing toolbox that is ready to use for verifying output from

- Function return values
- CLI stdout/stderr
- Filesystem changes

It is also flexible enough to build your own test harness like [trycmd](https://crates.io/crates/trycmd).

[§](https://docs.rs#which-tool-is-right)Which tool is right

- [cram](https://bitheap.org/cram/): End-to-end CLI snapshotting agnostic of any programming language- See also [scrut](https://github.com/facebookincubator/scrut)

- See also
- [trycmd](https://crates.io/crates/trycmd): For running a lot of blunt tests (limited test predicates)- Particular attention is given to allow the test data to be pulled into documentation, like
with [mdbook](https://rust-lang.github.io/mdBook/)

- Particular attention is given to allow the test data to be pulled into documentation, like
with
- [tryfn](https://crates.io/crates/tryfn): For running a lot of simple input/output tests
- `snapbox`: When you want something like- `trycmd`in one off cases or you need to customize- `trycmd`s behavior.
- [assert_cmd](https://crates.io/crates/assert_cmd)+- [assert_fs](https://crates.io/crates/assert_fs): Test cases follow a certain pattern but special attention is needed in how to verify the results.
- Hand-written test cases: for peculiar circumstances

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting Started

Testing Functions:

- `assert_data_eq!`

Testing Commands:

- `cmd::Command`
- `cmd::OutputAssert`- `Command`- `Output`

Testing Filesystem Interactions:

- `dir::DirRoot`
- `Assert`

You can also build your own version of these with the lower-level building blocks these are made of.

Feature Flags

- `detect-encoding`
- `dir`
- `path`- `dir`

- `examples`
- `regex`
- `json`

- `structured-data`
- `debug`

Default Feature Flags

- `diff`- *(enabled by default)*— Fancy diffs on failure
- `color`- *(enabled by default)*— Colored output support
- `color-auto`- *(enabled by default)*— Auto-detect whether to use colors
